title: Latency postmortem: VPC edge proxy serialization surges (deep dive) - Nyx Robotics
summary: Deep-dive postmortem on intermittent p95/p99 spikes observed from Nyx's VPC-edge deployment. Discussion covered serialization overhead at the edge proxy, streaming vs unary (non-streaming) tradeoffs, KV cache hotkeying, batching knobs, quantization impact, and suggested test harness + mitigations. Agreed next steps: share trace/kernels, run controlled cold-cache + multi-h3 hop test, pilot fallback topology, and update benchmark sheet.
next_steps: Redwood to share kernel-level traces + pprof flamegraphs (Samir)
Nyx to run cold-cache + long-tail simulated test and share results (Priya)
Schedule follow-up 90-minute bench run to validate fallback topology (by 2026-02-10)
Redwood to propose config patch for prefix caching TTL and adaptive-batching defaults
action_items: Samir: upload kernel traces + root cause sketch to shared folder (due 2026-02-05)
Priya: run cold-cache script across 3 zones, capture p50/p95/p99 and tcpdump (due 2026-02-08)
Liam: open internal ticket to test VPC route table + MTU settings (no date)
Jules: prepare a short demo of streaming fallthrough + non-streaming baseline (due 2026-02-09)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Navarro (Redwood SE), Ana Cortez (Redwood SA), Devon Li (Redwood SRE consultant); Marta Reyes (CTO - Nyx), Liam O'Connor (Platform Lead), Priya Singh (SRE), Oliver Chen (Infra)
Shared artifacts: Nyx-bench-2026-01.csv (benchmark sheet link), nyx-vpc-traces.tar.gz (kernel traces), rwin-opt-proposal.pdf (Redwood config proposal)

[00:00] Samir: ok hi everyone thanks for making time, this is the postmortem deep dive on the p95/p99 surges you saw last week, high level goal is to isolate whether the tail originates at the VPC edge proxy serialization step, or deeper in the serving runtime or kv/cache layer
[00:22] Marta: thanks Samir yeah we had a couple of production incidents where p99 spiked to ~420ms for generation requests that usually sit at p95 ~120ms so it's pretty painful for our UI flows
[00:35] Jules: to set expectations, we'll walk through the trace chunks you shared then map to likely hotspots: proxy serialization, network retransmits, kv cold lookups, or batching engine stalls
[00:50] Priya: quick note, our cluster is in a single VPC per region, edge proxies are envoy-based with a thin gRPC multiplexing layer; we do have MTU set to 1500, no jumbo frames
[01:05] Ana: got it. when you say "serialization" can you describe the proxy path? envoy receives the HTTP/1.1 chunk then translates to gRPC, there's an encode/decode step plus protobuf serialization which can add CPU on the proxy host, especially if small requests are bursty
[01:22] Oliver: yep and sometimes we see high CPU on the proxy pod during spikes, but not consistently correlated with the largest p99 windows which is odd
[01:35] Jules: interesting. in the traces I pulled there's a recurring pattern: a 10-25ms stub in the proxy encode, then a ~60-120ms one-way between edge & internal nic, then 100-300ms in serving queue at the host when the kv-cache miss happens. but there are traces where proxy cost is 150ms alone
[01:58] Marta: so multiple different modes then, hm
[02:10] Samir: yes, that's the tail's multimodal nature. some tails are "serialization-dominant" others are "kv-cold-miss-dominant". need to separate them in the bench.
[02:25] [02:26] Liam: question - are you seeing differences between streaming calls and unary (non-streaming) calls? our UI uses streaming for interactive completions but we also have internal batch endpoints that use unary
[02:40] Jules: good question. streaming keeps TCP connection open and tends to amortize TLS handshake/serialization cost for multi-token streams. unary calls re-establish or reuse short-lived connections and can hit costly serialize/deserialize more often. in your traces, streaming p95 was better than unary in baseline, but streaming had weird micro-spikes when proxy serialization fell behind
[03:05] Priya: we observed that after a traffic burst the first few streaming sessions had long cold starts then later stabilized - sounds like a kv warmup problem?
[03:18] Devon: likely. KV prefix caching + continuous batching interplay is subtle. If your prefix cache TTL is too short or cold-shard hotkeying occurs, initial requests can cascade into large KV misses which stall the infer host, causing backlog and amplifying the proxy CPU footprint
[03:38] [03:40] Jules: exact. we saw a pattern where a hot key eviction caused 200ms+ GC-style fetch to origin, and that single fetch serialized other requests in the same shard, increasing queueing 
[03:52] Oliver: btw we also run quantized model variants (int8) behind a quantization flag—could quantization explain variability? sometimes int8 runs faster but occasionally slower on certain GPUs due to kernel selection mismatches
[04:06] Ana: yes, quantized kernels can be faster on average but have sharper variance due to fallback to slower kernels on certain sequence lengths or when alignment isn't ideal. our runtime chooses kernels based on sequence length and hardware; sometimes it chooses a non-optimized path when shapes change unexpectedly
[04:26] Marta: can you expand on kernel selection mismatches?
[04:32] Jules: brief: the runtime has a kernel table. for a given architecture and sequence length distribution it picks a fast int8 kernel; if the input length crosses a boundary, or quant padding changes, we might trigger a different kernel with worse performance, esp at tail where shapes vary
[04:48] [05:00] Priya: that matches logs—some large inputs during the spike period had sequence length jitter which correlates with higher p99
[05:12] Samir: couple mitigation ideas we can try quickly: 1) stabilize batching boundaries by capping max token length and padding policy, 2) set prefix TTL longer for hot keys to reduce cold-miss storms, 3) enable streaming fallthrough to non-streaming fallback for specific paths, 4) pin the quantized kernel choice for the slow path while we investigate
[05:38] Liam: pinning kernel - would that force less optimal throughput? we worry about throughput regressions
[05:45] Jules: it could impact average throughput slightly but reduces variance. it's often a good short-term tradeoff when tail is killing UX
[05:52] [06:00] Marta: what about the VPC network hops and retransmits? we saw some TCP retransmits in the capture, maybe between edge and internal route table
[06:10] Devon: retransmits usually add linear delay. with p99, a single retransmit early in the request can add 50-200ms. if your path crosses a NAT gateway or transit gateway, that can add jitter. also, small MTUs with fragmentation on certain hops can blow up latency
[06:28] Oliver: there is a transit gateway in our topology for multi-account routing, we've suspected it as a variable
[06:35] Ana: a test: run the bench with route pinned inside the region (no transit), and also with jumbo frames enabled if NIC supports it — see if p99 changes. also get per-hop tcpdump/seq acks to know where retransmit originates
[06:50] [07:05] Samir: for the bench harness we recommend these tests: - cold-cache profile: clear prefix cache and run burst (10k reqs) - hot-cache steady state: run continuous steady load for 30m - single-hotkey storm: push requests to same key - streaming vs unary A/B: compare identical payloads via streaming vs unary - kernel pin test: force int8 kernel vs runtime auto-select
[07:32] Priya: what do you recommend for measurement? we've been capturing p50/p95/p99 but maybe need histograms over sub-second bins
[07:42] Jules: yes, sub-1ms bins for the proxy serialization step, 1-10ms bins for internal hop, and 10-100ms bins for serving queue. also capture per-token latency for streaming sessions (token emission times)
[07:56] [08:00] Liam: curious - you mentioned prefix caching TTL. what's a safe default? we currently expire at 30s
[08:07] Ana: A common pattern: increase to 5-10 minutes for stable prefixes. If memory pressure is concern, use LFU eviction heuristics for prefix cache rather than strict TTL. That reduces cold-miss storms without unbounded memory growth
[08:20] Marta: memory pressure is real for us, we can't just make TTL 10 minutes without eviction policies
[08:28] Jules: use weighted LFU with small TTL for very low-frequency prefixes and higher TTL for popular ones — Redwood can push a config suggestion for your workload mix
[08:40] [09:00] Priya: on batching, we see large variance when continuous batching tries to merge disparate requests. can we change batching window size?
[09:10] Devon: yes, two levers: max_batch_size and batch_hold_ms. Lowering hold_ms reduces latency but may reduce throughput. Adaptive policies that increase hold_ms only when throughput is underutilized help. Another lever is request shaping by size class — route small requests to a low-latency pool
[09:30] Jules: yep route small requests to low-latency dedicated lanes (dedicated capacity) or dedicate small-batch workers. Redwood supports multi-pool routing so we can propose a config
[09:42] [10:00] Marta: streaming fallthrough you mentioned earlier — can you describe?
[10:06] Samir: streaming fallthrough means: if the streaming path exceeds latency SLOs due to serialization backlog, we fall back to a unary fast-path that returns final payload sooner or a short-polling mechanism. It's a pragmatic trade — UX may be slightly different but far fewer tail glitches
[10:20] Priya: we worry about client compatibility and rework, but it could be staged behind a feature flag for specific routes
[10:28] Samir: yes, feature-flagged rollout recommended
[10:32] [10:40] Oliver: let's talk on-prem implications: if we move edge proxies on-prem or into a dedicated NIC with SR-IOV, would that reduce serialization overhead?
[10:50] Ana: SR-IOV and NIC offload reduce kernel and CPU hops, yes. If you can move the proxy onto hardware that supports checksum offload and larger MTU, you cut tail. However on-prem adds ops burden and you still need careful kernel/buffer settings
[11:05] Jules: also, on certain GPUs quantized kernels behave better on on-prem stacks with tuned drivers, so you might see more consistent int8 performance on-prem
[11:15] [11:30] Marta: OK this is a long list. what's the prioritization?
[11:34] Samir: 1) reproduce with controlled bench (cold vs hot vs hotkey storm) 2) collect tcpdump/tls traces + kernel pprof 3) short-term mitigations: prefix TTL bump, pin kernel for suspect hosts, reduce batch_hold_ms for latency-critical routes 4) medium-term: adaptive-batching + dedicated low-latency pool 5) long-term: topology review (transit gateway removal or route pinning) and optionally on-prem NIC offload
[12:00] [12:12] Priya: for the kernel traces, what granularity do you need? we can give per-process perf or eBPF stacks
[12:20] Jules: per-process with stacks collapsed by symbol is great plus eBPF tcp_event traces. pcap for the edge <-> compute path would help. we'll provide a trace-to-heatmap script that maps time windows to pipeline stages
[12:36] Samir: quick question on measurement: Nyx reported p95 ~120ms baseline, p99 ~420ms during incidents. what's an attainable p99 target after mitigations?
[12:50] Devon: with prefix caching + adaptive batching and small kernel pinning we think p99 ~200-250ms is achievable without sacrificing throughput; with network path pinning you can get lower ~150-180ms
[13:05] Marta: that's promising.
[13:10] [13:20] Oliver: any concerns about quantization quality when pinning kernels? we have an internal QA gate for hallucination metrics
[13:30] Ana: pinning kernel doesn't force quantization level change. it just forces a particular low-variance kernel for int8. you should run quality evals on a holdout prompt set; Redwood can run evals tied to your prompt set as part of the bench
[13:45] Samir: we'll pair the bench with small evals so we can catch regressions quickly
[13:50] [14:00] Priya: timeline — can Redwood prepare the config patch and bench script within 48 hours?
[14:06] Samir: yes we'll push scripts and a test harness. Jules will own the streaming vs unary A/B harness. Ana will write the cache policy suggestion. Devon will sketch kernel pin steps
[14:18] [14:30] Marta: wonderful. last question: cost tradeoffs — dedicted low-latency lanes and longer TTLs sound more expensive. can you estimate delta?
[14:40] Jules: rough ballpark: dedicated low-latency pool (small instance fleet) could be +8-12% on GPU cost but reduces tail-related user churn. Longer cache TTL is operational cost (RAM) but negligible in GPU dollars. We'll add a cost table to the config proposal
[14:58] Samir: ok let's move into the trace walk-through - Jules can share screen
[15:05] [15:10] Jules: sharing... looking at trace chunk 17: you can see a 180ms proxy encode (red), then a 90ms network hop, then a 240ms serving queue where a kv-miss origin fetch adds 150ms
[15:28] Priya: that map matches what we saw, so it's a composite tail
[15:35] Jules: note the smaller traces where proxy alone was 140-200ms — those aligned with high CPU on proxy hosts. we saw a correlation with other batch size spikes around the same time
[15:50] [16:00] Oliver: would increasing concurrency on proxy hosts help?
[16:05] Devon: it helps up to a point; if proxy CPU is the cause, scale horizontally or offload serialization to a sidecar in C/C++ (currently envoy filter is Lua/Python) - language matters. Or inject a tiny binary encoder nearer to NIC
[16:20] Ana: replacing high-overhead filters improves median and tail. envoy hot path should avoid heavy script processing when possible
[16:28] [16:40] Marta: good, we can run a scripted load on proxy with pprof and identify hotspots
[16:48] Samir: next up, we'll formalize the bench plan and share it along with the config patch. also we'll schedule the 90-minute bench for the week of 2026-02-08
[17:00] [17:15] Priya: one more thing — logging: our request IDs sometimes get stripped by the transit gateway which makes correlation hard; any tips?
[17:24] Jules: propagate request-id in a header and use a short-lived trace sampler for incidents. we can share a small logging shim to ensure the id survives the gateway
[17:35] Marta: perfect thanks
[17:40] Samir: ok we're almost out of time, quick recap and owners
[17:45] [17:46] Samir: recap: reproduce via bench, gather tcpdump/pprof, short-term TTL + kernel pin + batch_hold tweaks, schedule bench (owners in action items)
[18:00] Liam: sounds good. thanks everyone
[18:05] Jules: will follow up with the artifacts and the bench script, look for links in slack + the shared folder
[18:14] Marta: appreciate it, thanks Redwood
[18:20] [58:00] meeting end
